video.title: He Makes $4K/Day With This Weird Middleman Business

summary: William Lindholm describes a cake-sourcing and delivery business that helps companies get sales prospects’ attention with physical gifts. The business began as an automated employee birthday-cake service in Norway, then pivoted in the US to sales campaigns after birthday software proved difficult to sell at scale. William says the new model uses AI agents to find and negotiate with bakeries, while software coordinates large orders and tracks deliveries. The discussion emphasizes attention, measurable sales outcomes, and the need to keep testing which gifts produce meetings and closed sales.

speakers.name: William Lindholm
speakers.description: Founder of the cake-delivery and corporate gifting business discussed in the interview.

ideas.name: Cold-cake sales gifting and delivery
ideas.one_liner: Coordinate local bakeries, physical cake deliveries and tracking so B2B customers can use gifts to get sales prospects’ attention.
ideas.business_model: Bulk per-cake sales campaigns with logistics and software layered over a network of local bakeries; exact fee structure is not stated.
ideas.customer: Companies selling higher-value products or services, including software businesses, agencies, accountants and real estate brokers.
ideas.problem: Sales outreach is easy to ignore amid email, calls and digital noise; companies want more attention and booked meetings.
ideas.offer: Source suitable bakeries, negotiate discounts, coordinate cakes across locations, let clients enter recipients and track orders, and provide delivery photos. The client can pair the cake with its own pitch and follow-up.

pricing.model: Per cake at bulk campaign volume; any separate software or management fee is not stated.

price_points.label: Bulk-volume price described by the host

pricing.notes: The host gives the per-cake range and William agrees; the transcript does not clarify how much is charged by the business versus paid to the bakery.

acquisition_channels.details: A cake stunt for venture capital firms went viral, generated news coverage and led to inbound interest. Clients may also post photos of campaigns, creating further attention and inquiries.

quote.text: And that gives you PR and then they might think, oh, this worked on me because I just booked the meeting and posted it on social media.
quote.speaker: William Lindholm

acquisition_channels.details: William says people who received cakes have contacted the business to ask about doing campaigns themselves.

quote.text: Like I'm getting in bonds from people that have caught in a cake and think this is cool.

acquisition_channels.details: PR and news coverage brought inbound after a cake campaign attracted attention. The current business's precise ongoing customer-acquisition process is not stated.

quote.text: That hit the news and we got so many in-bouts.
quote.speaker: William Lindholm

ideas.delivery: A client supplies recipient details; the business routes orders to bakeries in relevant locations, coordinates the deliveries, and provides tracking and delivery photos. Local bakeries make and physically deliver most cakes. William says they sometimes send a cake by plane when a suitable local bakery is unavailable. The client handles its own sales conversation and follow-up.
unit_economics_claims: William says a bulk campaign price is in the $50–$70 range per cake, as restated by the host.
William says the business negotiates a 30% discount with bakeries; the transcript presents this as the requested discount, not a confirmed average.
William reports $120,000 revenue and $30,000–$40,000 profit in a month.
tools: AI agent for sourcing and negotiating with bakeries
Order-entry and tracking system for recipients and deliveries
ideas.time_to_first_revenue: The US operation had zero sales for its first two and a half months; after a viral campaign, William says the pivot was about six weeks old when monthly revenue reached $120,000.

acquisition.how: Inbound interest from viral campaigns, PR and referrals can be routed automatically, but creating attention and building trust still require deliberate campaigns and human judgment.

onboarding.how: A system accepts recipient lists and campaign details, while staff may need to check addresses, locations, timing and special requests.

delivery.how: Agents can source suppliers and coordinate orders, but baking, quality checks and physical delivery depend on people and local bakeries.

billing.how: Bulk orders and invoicing could be processed with software, but the transcript does not describe the payment or invoicing workflow.

support.how: Order tracking can answer routine questions, but delayed or failed physical deliveries and cake-quality issues need human resolution.

uk_applicability.notes: A local bakery network and B2B gifting service could operate in the UK. Cold marketing emails to limited companies may be used subject to applicable rules; unsolicited electronic marketing to individuals and sole traders requires consent, and cold calls must be screened against TPS/CTPS. Physical delivery and bakery coverage remain local constraints.

risks: Physical delivery and cake quality are outside full software control; poor execution can damage the client's reputation.
The business can become operationally overloaded when many locations and large orders arrive at once.
The cake format may lose novelty if prospects receive too many gifts.
The claimed meeting conversion does not show whether meetings become customers or justify campaign costs.
UK prospecting emails, calls and recipient-data handling need to follow applicable marketing and privacy rules.

tactics.name: Lead with a surprising gift in a cold-call pitch
steps: Call a relevant business contact and open with a specific, unexpected gift rather than a generic product pitch.
Offer the gift in exchange for a meeting, then explain the underlying service.
Track meeting bookings and compare the result with prior outreach.

quote.text: we would like to give you a free cake if you'd like to take a meeting with us.
quote.speaker: William Lindholm

tactics.name: Tie the offer to a budget connected to revenue
steps: Identify whether the buyer's budget is tied to sales or engineering rather than a lower-priority employee benefit.
Frame the gift campaign as a way to start more sales conversations.
Test the offer with the buyer before building extensive integrations or infrastructure.

quote.text: You always wanna sell your product and get more customers and you always wanna build your product better so you get more customers.
quote.speaker: William Lindholm

tactics.name: Use a memorable campaign to create a PR loop
steps: Make the campaign visually distinctive enough for recipients to photograph or share.
Ask clients to track whether recipients post the gift and whether those posts create inquiries.
Use resulting media coverage and inbound interest to attract more campaign customers.

quote.text: And that gives you PR and then they might think, oh, this worked on me because I just booked the meeting and posted it on social media.
quote.speaker: William Lindholm

tactics.name: Measure downstream sales outcomes, not only meetings
steps: Track how many gifts produce meetings.
Ask customers to compare close rates for gift-led meetings with their other meetings.
Collect enough data to compare campaign costs with close rates and revenue before making strong ROI claims.
